question: For the unoptimized reference loader, `prepareCircuit_ryCount` gives RY count 2^n - 1 and `prepareCircuit_cxCount` gives CX count 2*(2^n - 1 - n). reference_answer: The loader is a chronological low-bit-first binary tree: at each of the n levels it applies a uniformly controlled RY on the newly added highest wire, controlled on all lower wires. The RY count 2^n - 1 counts exactly one RY per INTERNAL node of the full binary tree over n bits: level k (0-indexed) contributes 2^k rotations, and sum_{k=0}^{n-1} 2^k = 2^n - 1. question: Let H = C^d with the standard inner product of Eq. (2.4), and let |psi> in H be a unit vector, <psi|psi> = 1. Define rho := |psi><psi|. Starting only from Definition 2.1 (a quantum state is a density operator with rho >= 0 and tr rho = 1), prove that rho is a legitimate quantum state, that it is a rank-one orthogonal projector (rho^2 = rho = rho^dagger), and explain in what precise sense this makes rho an extreme point (pure state) of the convex set of density operators. State explicitly which step uses normalization of |psi> and why dropping it breaks the trace condition.
reference_answer: Hermiticity: rho^dagger = (|psi><psi|)^dagger = |psi><psi| = rho. Positivity: for any |phi>, <phi|rho|phi> = <phi|psi><psi|phi> = |<psi|phi>|^2 >= 0, hence rho >= 0. Trace/normalization: in any orthonormal basis, tr rho = sum_i <e_i|psi><psi|e_i> = <psi|(sum_i |e_i><e_i|)|psi> = <psi|psi> = 1, where the final equality is exactly the unit-norm hypothesis computed with the Eq. (2.4) inner product. Both Definition 2.1 conditions hold, so rho is a quantum state. Idempotency: rho^2 = |psi><psi|psi><psi| = <psi|psi>|psi><psi| = rho, so rho is an orthogonal projector onto the one-dimensional span{|psi>}, hence rank 1. Extreme point: if rho = p sigma_1 + (1-p) sigma_2 with 0<p<1 and density operators sigma_i, positivity forces the range of each sigma_i inside range(rho) = span{|psi>}; the only trace-one state supported on a one-dimensional space is |psi><psi|, so sigma_1 = sigma_2 = rho and the decomposition is trivial. Thus rho is an extreme point (pure state), matching the text's statement that a pure density matrix has rank 1 and equals a projector |psi><psi|. If normalization were dropped (<psi|psi> = c != 1) then tr rho = c != 1 violates Definition 2.1, Idempotency becomes rho^2=c rho: it fails for nonzero psi with c!=1, but the zero vector gives the zero idempotent, which still has trace0 and is not a state. Only for c>0 may one renormalize rho=|psi><psi|/c; the zero vector has no normalized state representative.

Computing the (|0^m,0^a>) block of W, the prepare amplitudes sqrt(alpha_j)/sqrt(gamma) on each side contract through U_SEL to weight term j by (sqrt(alpha_j)/sqrt(gamma))^2 = alpha_j/gamma, giving <0^m,0^a|W|0^m,0^a> = sum_j (alpha_j/gamma) B_j (Eq. 9.41). question: Proposition 9.12 (Lin-Wiebe, p.150) block-encodes a product A_{M-1}...A_0 by applying U_{A_j} in BE_{alpha_j, a_j}(A_j, eps_j) sequentially on disjoint ancilla registers and a common system register, yielding U in BE_{prod_j alpha_j, sum_j a_j}(A_{M-1}...A_0, prod_j (alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_j alpha_j). Prove the error bound by induction on M, using ||B_j|| <= 1 and ||A_j|| <= alpha_j+eps_j. Then contrast this multiplicative error growth with the additive error of the sum construction (Prop. 9.10) and explain the resource meaning of disjoint ancilla registers. Assume alpha_j>0, eps_j>=0; when using a first-order relative-error approximation, explicitly require all eps_j/alpha_j small (fixed M).
reference_answer: For each j set B_j := <0^{a_j}|U_{A_j}|0^{a_j}>, so ||A_j - alpha_j B_j|| <= eps_j, ||B_j|| <= 1, and ||A_j|| <= ||A_j - alpha_j B_j|| + alpha_j||B_j|| <= alpha_j+eps_j. Disjoint ancillas make the all-zero ancilla block factorize: <0^{a_0+...+a_{M-1}}|U|0^{...}> = B_{M-1}...B_0 (Eq. 9.45). We prove ||prod_j A_j - prod_j (alpha_j B_j)|| <= prod_j(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_j alpha_j by induction on M. Base M=1: ||A_0 - alpha_0 B_0|| <= eps_0 = (alpha_0+eps_0) - alpha_0. Step: let P = prod_{j<=M-2}A_j, P~ = prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j B_j). Then ||A_{M-1}P - (alpha_{M-1}B_{M-1})P~|| <= ||(A_{M-1}-alpha_{M-1}B_{M-1})P|| + ||alpha_{M-1}B_{M-1}(P-P~)|| <= eps_{M-1}||P|| + alpha_{M-1}||P-P~||. With ||P|| <= prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) and the induction hypothesis ||P-P~|| <= prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_{j<=M-2}alpha_j, this is <= eps_{M-1}prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) + alpha_{M-1}[prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_{j<=M-2}alpha_j] = (alpha_{M-1}+eps_{M-1})prod_{j<=M-2}(alpha_j+eps_j) - alpha_{M-1}prod_{j<=M-2}alpha_j = prod_j(alpha_j+eps_j) - prod_j alpha_j, completing the induction. Contrast: the sum (Prop. 9.10) has additive error sum_j eps_j and additive subnormalization gamma=sum_j alpha_j; the product has multiplicative subnormalization prod_j alpha_j and error prod(alpha_j+eps_j)-prod alpha_j, which for small eps_j is approximately (prod alpha_j) sum_j (eps_j/alpha_j) -- relative errors add while absolute error is amplified by the product of subnormalizations. Disjoint ancilla registers: each factor keeps its own a_j ancillas (not reused), so total ancilla cost is sum_j a_j; disjointness is exactly what lets the zero-ancilla block factor into B_{M-1}...B_0. This is simple but not ancilla-optimal (the text notes Example 11.9/Fig. 9.6 reduces a two-factor product to a+1 ancillas via deferred measurement). The relative-error comparison is a first-order expansion for fixed M with positive alpha_j and small eps_j/alpha_j; it is not an identity. The exact product-minus-product estimate is the theorem.

question: Consider the two-qubit EPR/Bell state |Phi+>_AB = (1/sqrt 2)(|0>_A|0>_B + |1>_A|1>_B) with density matrix Phi+_AB = |Phi+><Phi+| as in Eqs. (2.17)-(2.18). Using the defining relation Eq. (2.14), tr(rho_AB (X_A tensor 1_B)) = tr(rho_A X_A) for all X_A, and/or the basis formula Eq. (2.15), compute the marginal rho_A = tr_B Phi+_AB and show rho_A = (1/2) 1 (Eq. (2.22)). Explain why this maximally mixed marginal shows Phi+ is not a product state, and why the partial trace is independent of the orthonormal basis chosen in Eq. (2.15).
reference_answer: Write |Phi+> = (1/sqrt2) sum_{i in {0,1}} |i>_A|i>_B. Using Eq. (2.15) with the computational B-basis: tr_B Phi+_AB = sum_k (1_A tensor <k|_B) |Phi+><Phi+| (1_A tensor |k>_B). Since (1_A tensor <k|_B)|Phi+> = (1/sqrt2)|k>_A, each term is (1/2)|k>_A<k|_A, and summing over k in {0,1} gives rho_A = (1/2)(|0><0| + |1><1|) = (1/2)1, the maximally mixed state (Eq. 2.22). Equivalently via Eq. (2.14): tr(Phi+_AB (X_A tensor 1_B)) = (1/2)(<0|X_A|0> + <1|X_A|1>) = (1/2) tr X_A = tr((1/2)1 X_A) for all X_A, so by uniqueness rho_A = (1/2)1. Not a product state: a pure global state has a pure marginal iff it is a product; here rho_A = (1/2)1 is maximally mixed (eigenvalues 1/2,1/2, rank 2), so if Phi+ = omega_A tensor sigma_B its A-marginal would be the pure omega_A, contradicting rho_A = (1/2)1. A pure global state with a mixed marginal is by definition entangled. Basis independence: Eq. (2.14) defines rho_A uniquely by its action against all X_A with no reference to a basis; Eq. (2.15) merely evaluates that unique operator, so every orthonormal {|e_i>_B} yields the same rho_A, as the text explicitly notes.

Wording by definition is imprecise but argument preserves this essential pure-global premise.
